title: A rocket booster you can fly

stops.caption: A real booster, flying on real physics
stops.detail: It lights a moment after it appears and climbs on its own thrust. The tanks drain as it burns, the pad falls away, and the plume widens as the air thins.
points: Click an engine to shut it down
Throttle and time speed are below

stops.caption: Two tanks: oxygen on top, kerosene below
stops.detail: It carries its own oxygen, so it can burn where there is no air. About 2.45 kg of liquid oxygen burns with each kg of RP-1 kerosene; 400 tonnes of the two are nearly 80% of the rocket.
points: a pipe (the downcomer) runs LOX down through the kerosene tank
watch the levels drop as it burns

stops.caption: Nine engines share the work
stops.detail: Each makes about 0.85 MN at sea level, rising to 0.91 MN in vacuum. Click one to shut it down: thrust drops by a ninth, the plume shortens, and the climb slows -- but it can still make it.
points: engine-out tolerance is why boosters cluster engines
they throttle down to 40% to ease off through max-Q

stops.caption: The turbopump: a jet engine just to move fuel
stops.detail: Propellant has to enter the chamber at over 100 bar, faster than tank pressure can push it. A gas generator burns a little of it to spin a turbine at ~36,000 rpm, which drives the oxygen and fuel pumps on the same shaft.
points: gas-generator cycle: the turbine exhaust is dumped overboard (the small side plume)
a few % of the flow is spent this way

stops.caption: Injector and chamber: where it burns
stops.detail: The injector sprays oxygen and kerosene into the chamber in fine jets that mix and burn at ~3,600 K and ~97 bar. The kerosene first runs through channels in the nozzle walls to cool them -- that is why the walls glow.
points: the gas here moves slowly, Mach ~0.1
regenerative cooling: fuel takes the heat back in

stops.caption: The nozzle turns heat into speed
stops.detail: The chamber squeezes the gas through a narrow throat, where it reaches exactly the speed of sound, then lets it expand in the bell. Expanding, it cools and speeds up to Mach ~3.5 -- about 3 km/s. Watch the particles accelerate past the throat.

stops.caption: The plume changes with height
stops.detail: At sea level the air pushes harder than the exhaust, squeezing the plume narrow into shock diamonds. Higher up the exhaust's own pressure wins and the plume balloons outward -- and the same engine makes more thrust.
points: lower outside pressure pₐ → more thrust

stops.caption: What it all adds up to
stops.detail: Thrust fights gravity and drag while the rocket gets lighter every second, so it accelerates harder as it climbs. Drag peaks at max-Q around a minute in, then the air thins away. When the propellant runs out (main engine cutoff) it coasts up to its apogee.
points: Isp ≈ 282 s at sea level, 311 s in vacuum

stops.caption: Fly it again
stops.detail: Reset and launch: try 40% throttle, three engines out, or 20× time to watch the whole burn to apogee.

summary: A liquid-fuelled booster with nine engines on a gas-generator cycle, flown by a vertical-flight simulation: thrust from mass flow and exhaust pressure against falling air pressure, drag, and gravity, with propellant drained at the real mass flow.
